paragraphs.source_en: The study of the relationship between the landscape and the Round Head art has not been fully explored and except for general statements about the topography of several sites, little information has been given regarding this fundamental aspect. Lhote (1958), Hachid (1998) Mori (2000) and Soleilhavoup (2007) mentioned the probable use of the Tassilian sites as sanctuaries or sacred places. Sansoni (1994) developed this argument postulating the existence of Primary Centres where human frequentation was uninterrupted and intense, which is reflected in the number of painted walls and the styles represented. Less important would be Secondary Centres with intermittent or limited frequentation, where paintings are not abundant and they are represented by only a few Round Head styles.

paragraphs.source_en: According to Sansoni (1994), the most important cultic centre of the whole period was Sefar in the Tassili, which contained all the existing styles and also unique styles present only in this site. The second Primary Centre was Jabbaren with minor number of images and styles. All the remaining sites would then be Secondary Centres.

paragraphs.source_en: The Round Head paintings occur in a variety of environments. The essential conditions for image-making were the presence of suitable rock walls; however, not every suitable wall was painted. In the Tassili, there are frequent situations in which a wall contains numerous images but the next wall, equally suitable for paintings, is totally empty. The same is applicable for entire sites especially in the Tassili; whereas in one stone city paintings are abundant, the next site is often completely devoid of any rock art even though it possesses suitable shelters. Jabbaren, for example, is a stone city on a hill, crossed by a narrow wadi. However, the paintings are all accumulated in the southern part of the site whereas the northern side contains no images at all despite there being equally suitable shelters.
